lessons.title: Read the Nano and use its five navigation buttons
lessons.summary: Follow the screen labels, highlight a menu choice and return without changing a condition.
prerequisites: Use the fictional FINDR Nano training site.
The scrolling practice PIN is 2468; real installations use their own authorised access arrangements.

steps.title: Read the normal indications
steps.explanation: Find the green Power indication and read the system status. A quiet buzzer alone does not prove normal operation.
steps.expected: No fire, fault, disablement or test is active.
steps.commonMistake: Read the current selection and its label before pressing the highlighted physical key.

steps.title: Open the main menu
steps.explanation: Press the physical left soft key labelled Menu. The four top-level branches are Logs, User, Settings and Engineering.
steps.expected: The main screen and intended selection are displayed.
steps.commonMistake: Read the current selection and its label before pressing the highlighted physical key.

steps.title: Select User
steps.explanation: Use Next until User is highlighted, then use the left Select button.
steps.expected: The user screen and intended selection are displayed.
steps.commonMistake: Read the current selection and its label before pressing the highlighted physical key.

steps.title: Open System
steps.explanation: Select System from the User menu. Read the Code, Weekly Test, Day Night Mode and Display Test options.
steps.expected: The user system screen and intended selection are displayed.
steps.commonMistake: Read the current selection and its label before pressing the highlighted physical key.

steps.title: Back out one level
steps.explanation: The right soft key now means Back. Return without applying an operation.
steps.expected: The User menu is visible.
steps.commonMistake: Read the current selection and its label before pressing the highlighted physical key.

steps.title: Return to the normal display
steps.explanation: Use the displayed Back selections to return to status. Opening a menu did not change protection.
steps.expected: The status screen and intended selection are displayed.
steps.commonMistake: Read the current selection and its label before pressing the highlighted physical key.

steps.title: Check the unchanged result
steps.explanation: Confirm that only the normal indications remain.
steps.expected: The panel is normal and the menus are closed.
steps.commonMistake: Read the current selection and its label before pressing the highlighted physical key.

lessons.restoreInstruction: Check the displayed state before leaving the lesson.

lessons.title: Enter the scrolling Customer Mode PIN
lessons.summary: Practise plus/minus, Next and Accept instead of a numeric keypad.
prerequisites: Use the fictional FINDR Nano training site.
The scrolling practice PIN is 2468; real installations use their own authorised access arrangements.

steps.title: Open the Customer Code form
steps.explanation: Use Menu → User → System → Code. Nano selects menu choices with Next and the left Select button.
steps.expected: The four-position User Access Code form is open.
steps.commonMistake: Read the current selection and its label before pressing the highlighted physical key.

steps.title: Set the four practice digits
steps.explanation: Set 2468 with plus/minus and Next. Every highlighted key is a real control that you press yourself. This is FINDR’s invented practice code.
steps.expected: All four intended digits are entered; access has not yet been granted.
steps.commonMistake: Trying to type 2468 on a numeric keypad, or treating this practice code as a real-site code.

steps.title: Accept the practice PIN
steps.explanation: Read the digits and select Accept with the left soft key. The panel returns in Customer Mode.
steps.expected: Customer Mode is active. No alarm or disablement operation has been automatically performed.
steps.commonMistake: Read the current selection and its label before pressing the highlighted physical key.

steps.title: Confirm Customer Mode
steps.explanation: Read the mode indication. Access has changed; the healthy training system itself has not.
steps.expected: Access Level 2 is active and the panel remains normal.
steps.commonMistake: Read the current selection and its label before pressing the highlighted physical key.

steps.title: Log out deliberately
steps.explanation: At the status screen, the right soft key shows Logout. End the practice session.
steps.expected: Customer Mode is ended; the same normal condition remains.
steps.commonMistake: Read the current selection and its label before pressing the highlighted physical key.

lessons.restoreInstruction: Check the displayed state before leaving the lesson.

steps.commonMistake: Read the current selection and its label before pressing the highlighted physical key.

lessons.restoreInstruction: This lesson leaves the simulated fire and sounders active. Continue with Silence and resound, then Reset after clearing the input.

steps.title: Identify the first fire
steps.explanation: The first event is Reception D1 in zone 1. Later events occur in the ground-floor offices and at the first-floor stair MCP.
steps.expected: Three fire events are active.
steps.commonMistake: Read the current selection and its label before pressing the highlighted physical key.

steps.title: Scroll one later event
steps.explanation: Use plus while the status display is showing the fires. The first fire stays at the top.

steps.commonMistake: Read the current selection and its label before pressing the highlighted physical key.

steps.title: Scroll back

steps.commonMistake: Read the current selection and its label before pressing the highlighted physical key.

steps.title: Inspect the active Fire log

steps.expected: The active Fire log is displayed.
steps.commonMistake: Read the current selection and its label before pressing the highlighted physical key.

steps.title: Separate sequence from count

steps.expected: Three fire entries remain active.
steps.commonMistake: Read the current selection and its label before pressing the highlighted physical key.

lessons.restoreInstruction: This lesson intentionally leaves the three simulated inputs active. Choose a new scenario or clear each input before a reset exercise.

helpArticles.title: Which Nano am I practising?
helpArticles.summary: The selected model is the GENT NANO-24 with V3.xx customer operation.
helpArticles.body:
The Nano has a single loop and its own five-button navigation row. Its 16 zone lamps and vertical face are different from the full-size Vigilon trainer. This module follows operating instructions 4188-947 issue 9, December 2021, with V3.xx installation instructions as a hardware cross-check.

FINDR supplies an invented building, device labels, events and a practice PIN. Where an older V2.xx commissioning document supplies additional detail, that version limit is shown. Physical-panel and firmware verification remains outstanding.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Treating the shared GENT name as proof that a Vigilon key sequence also applies to Nano.

helpArticles.title: What does normal look like?
helpArticles.summary: Read the status and lamps together; silence alone does not establish normal operation.
helpArticles.body:
With no fire, fault, disablement or test condition, the Nano shows its system message and the green Power indicator. The message can identify Customer Mode after authorised access.

A quiet buzzer can coexist with an active fire or fault, and silent sounders can coexist with a latched fire. Before finishing a training task, check the displayed counts and the Disablement and Test lamps as well as the sound.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Finishing because the noise has stopped while a disablement or test remains.

helpArticles.title: What do the five navigation buttons do?
helpArticles.summary: Two soft keys select current labels; Next moves the selection; minus and plus adjust a range.
helpArticles.body:
The left and right soft keys take their meaning from the bottom of the LCD. Their labels can be Menu, Select, Back, Accept, Save, Quit, Yes or No. Read the label each time.

The middle Next/Verify button moves to the next menu option or form position. Minus and plus change a selected number or other value. Next/Verify has an additional fire-delay role only when that option is available. A Nano has no numeric keypad for direct PIN entry.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Pressing plus to move between fields, or assuming the left soft key always means Save.

helpArticles.title: Save, Quit and Back are different
helpArticles.summary: A changed draft is applied with Save; Quit discards the form entries.
helpArticles.body:
Treat the visible form as a draft until Save is deliberately selected. For example, changing a zone status to Disabled without saving must not count as an actual disablement. Quit leaves the form without applying the edited entries.

Back takes you out of a menu level. Reopen a form and check the saved state when uncertain. FINDR hints rebuild the required selection and draft after a detour; they never press Save for you.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Seeing Disabled in an edited field and assuming the system has already been disabled.

helpArticles.title: Enter Customer Mode with a scrolling PIN
helpArticles.summary: Each PIN position is selected with Next and adjusted with minus or plus.
helpArticles.body:
Use Menu → User → System → Code. Adjust the selected digit, move to the next position and repeat until all four digits are entered. Select Accept to submit the code. The trainer uses 2468 solely as an invented practice code.

Real installations have their own authorised access arrangements. If an alarm-control button first requests the PIN, entering it enables the controls; then press the intended control again. The Nano quick reference explicitly shows this sequence for Silence Alarms.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Waiting for the originally requested alarm operation to happen automatically as soon as the code is accepted.

helpArticles.title: Why can my real panel show a read-only device?
helpArticles.summary: Device and channel disablement access is a commissioned setting.
helpArticles.body:
The current operating manual presents device and channel status as read-only information in Customer Mode. The older commissioning instructions document device and channel disablement at Level 3 by default, with a selectable Level 2 arrangement.

FINDR explicitly models a fictional site configured to allow these two operations in Customer Mode. This is an additional, version-limited training assumption, not a statement that every V3.xx panel allows it. Zone, sector and Other Alarms procedures have their own documented Customer Mode routes.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Assuming the practice fixture changes the access policy or firmware of a real panel.

helpArticles.title: What happens during Display Test?
helpArticles.summary: The display, lamps and buzzer are exercised for approximately eight seconds.
helpArticles.body:
From Customer Mode select Menu → User → System → Display Test. Observe the display clearing, the indicator lamps lighting and the buzzer sounding, then allow the panel to return to its system status.

This is a test of panel indications. It does not demonstrate that every detector, field sounder, cable or external interface works. The trainer keeps the documented duration separate from the shorter Vigilon display test.

During a guided lesson FINDR pauses simulation time while you read. The labelled eight-second training control advances the test deliberately. In free practice the timer runs while the Nano module is visible. The pause is a learning aid, not a real-panel function.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Treating a successful display test as a complete test of the installed fire alarm system.

helpArticles.title: Read the loop map before opening a device
helpArticles.summary: The displayed label and address identify a point; indentation can show a spur.
helpArticles.body:
Use Menu → User → Loop → Devices. The loop map lists the connected devices. Select the required row to open Device Details and check the label, type, state and zone assignment when shown.

The operator illustration uses a plus marker for SAFE-addressed devices and indentation for devices on a spur. These symbols are topology and addressing information; they are not a new zone number. FINDR uses seven invented devices on its single loop.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Using a similar label without checking the device address and type.

helpArticles.title: Disable and restore one device
helpArticles.summary: Choose a particular device, change its permitted status, save and confirm the result.
helpArticles.body:
In the configured FINDR fixture, open User → Loop → Devices and the intended Device Details form. Check the address and label, move to the status field, select Disabled and Save. The matching restoration exercise selects Enabled and saves again.

Disabling one device does not mean disabling its whole zone. A sounder-capable device can also produce a Sounder Disablement indication. The device-status edit is explicitly based on the optional Customer Mode configuration described in the older commissioning source.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Disabling a whole zone because it has the same number as the intended device.

helpArticles.title: What exactly does disabling a Nano zone remove?
helpArticles.summary: The selected Nano manual says both sensors and manual call points in that zone cease detecting fires.
helpArticles.body:
Use Menu → User → Zones and select the intended zone. The Status and Test fields are separate. To disable the zone, change Status to Disabled and Save; to restore it, choose Enabled and Save.

The V3.xx operating instructions explicitly include manual call points in a disabled zone. This behaviour must not be borrowed from a different panel family. An independently disabled device still needs its own restoration even after its zone is re-enabled.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Assuming manual call points in the disabled zone remain in service.

helpArticles.title: Zone or sector: which part are you changing?
helpArticles.summary: A zone groups detection; a sector controls alarm or plant outputs according to its configuration.
helpArticles.body:
The Sectors form is under Menu → User → Alarms → Sectors. Check the sector number, label, activation control and current state before changing Status Control. Saving Disabled prevents that sector from activating its associated alarm devices in a fire.

The Disablement and Sounder Disablement indicators identify this output-side condition. Re-enable the same sector and confirm the indication clears. A sector number is not interchangeable with a device or detection-zone number.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Selecting sector 2 when the intended isolation was a detector in zone 2.

helpArticles.title: Master Alarms, Fire Relay and Evacuate Input
helpArticles.summary: Other Alarms contains three separately saved enable states.
helpArticles.body:
Use Menu → User → Alarms → Other. Each row shows its current state and its enable status. Move through the three editable enable fields with Next and adjust only the intended row. Save commits the form; Quit abandons its edits.

Master Alarms disablement also lights Sounder Disablement. Do not treat a disabled fire relay or evacuate input as an equivalent operation: they affect different functions. The restoration check needs to read every row you changed.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Changing the correct value on the wrong row because the cursor position was overlooked.

helpArticles.title: Why is Disablement still lit after Reset?
helpArticles.summary: Reset deals with the fire condition; it is not a command to enable disabled functions.
helpArticles.body:
Use the active Disablement log to identify what is still out of service. Devices, zones, sectors, master alarms and other disabled functions have their own control routes. Re-enable the intended item and then recheck the active log.

A completed disablement lesson intentionally leaves its target disabled and offers the matching restoration exercise. FINDR does not silently restore the target as part of the completion celebration.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Repeatedly pressing Reset instead of locating and restoring the actual disabled item.

helpArticles.title: Cancel Buzzer and Silence Alarms do different jobs
helpArticles.summary: One stops the panel buzzer; the other controls the alarm sounders.
helpArticles.body:
Cancel Buzzer quietens the panel’s internal attention signal. It does not erase the event and does not, by itself, silence the building’s alarm sounders. Silence Alarms acts on alarm sounders after Customer Mode access.

The buzzer access level is configurable; this fictional training site uses the documented Level 2 arrangement. Check the remaining display and lamps after using either control.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Calling a fire cleared because the panel buzzer is quiet.

helpArticles.title: Read FIRST FIRE and later fire events
helpArticles.summary: The first fire remains at the top; later events are shown below and can be scrolled.
helpArticles.body:
The panel keeps the first fire visible to preserve its location and sequence. The first zone’s lamp flashes; subsequent zones in fire show steady zone indications. Use minus and plus to inspect the additional events.

The displayed count is not the same as the number of failed devices. Master Alarm or sector disablement information can replace the Total Fires line, so check the rest of the display as well.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Assuming the lower, most recently visible event is the first source of the fire condition.

helpArticles.title: Silence and resound the alarms
helpArticles.summary: Customer Mode gives access to the separate Silence Alarms and Sound Alarms controls.
helpArticles.body:
In the training scenario, cancel the local buzzer separately, use Silence Alarms and observe that the fire remains displayed. Use Sound Alarms to resound the alarm outputs.

This distinction also matters outside a fire event: Sound Alarms is a deliberate alarm command, not an acknowledgement button. The trainer’s rising lesson tones are learning feedback and are separate from the simulated alarm state.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Pressing Sound Alarms when the intended action was to acknowledge the panel buzzer.

helpArticles.title: Why does a fire return after Reset?
helpArticles.summary: The source condition must be cleared before the panel can return to normal.
helpArticles.body:
A still-operated manual call point, continuing detector stimulus or active fire input can cause the fire indication to return after Reset. In FINDR, the explicit simulated-input control represents clearing that fictional cause. It is separate from the physical Reset button.

The reset lesson first demonstrates a continuing cause, then clears the input and lets you press Reset again. Disablements are retained and need their own restoration.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Using Reset as a substitute for investigating and clearing the source of an event.

helpArticles.title: Read a fault without confusing acknowledgement and repair
helpArticles.summary: Cancelling the buzzer leaves the fault present until its cause is resolved.
helpArticles.body:
Read the fault message, device or circuit details and the count. Power Fault, Sounder Fault and System Fault add information to the common Fault indication. Review the active Fault log if several events are present.

The training controls can remove an invented fault cause so you can observe restoration. They do not suggest that pressing a menu button repairs a cable, supply or device on a real system.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Assuming the fault was fixed when its buzzer stopped.

helpArticles.title: Make sense of common fault phrases
helpArticles.summary: Use the complete message to decide which part of the installation needs investigation.
helpArticles.body:
Mains supply failed and battery-related messages point to power conditions. Lost Device identifies lost loop communication. A Master Alarm open/short message concerns a monitored alarm circuit; an interface-channel open/short message concerns that interface input circuit.

Loop Wiring changed SC identifies a short-circuit condition. Sensor out of specification identifies a device that is not functioning to specification. These messages guide investigation; none, alone, proves a single component is the cause.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Replacing a panel because a field circuit or device-specific fault appeared on its LCD.

helpArticles.title: Active logs show conditions that remain present
helpArticles.summary: Select Fire, Fault, Disablement or Test under Logs → Active.
helpArticles.body:
The active logs separate the kinds of current event. Fire and fault entries tell you which conditions are being reported; Disablement shows what remains out of service; Test shows zones currently in test. Use minus and plus to inspect additional entries.

A restored condition can disappear from an active log while remaining in Historic. The log view is observational: opening or scrolling it does not acknowledge, disable, restore or reset anything.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Reading an old history entry as proof that its condition is still active.

helpArticles.title: Historic event 1 is the newest
helpArticles.summary: Historic records provide a sequence, not a list of current faults only.
helpArticles.body:
Use Logs → Historic → View. The event numbered 1 is the most recent entry. Move through the list and read the time, date and event details together. The older V2.xx commissioning source gives a 999-event history capacity; FINDR uses that documented training bound while the selected V3.xx operator manual does not restate the capacity.

FINDR records its invented operations so you can compare a disablement with its later enable event, or an active fire with a reset. The older Vigilon trainer has a different log capacity; that value is not reused here.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Reading the oldest item first because its list number is larger.

helpArticles.title: Why may Print be absent?
helpArticles.summary: Printing depends on an attached, configured printer and the relevant access level.
helpArticles.body:
The operator procedures condition Print on the panel’s printer arrangement. Historic printing uses a first and last event range; active-log printing prints the relevant active entries. A missing Print option does not establish that the menu map is wrong.

This training fixture has no physical printer. Printer-related routes are identified as configuration-dependent reference material rather than producing a fictitious real print job.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Expecting a printer-dependent choice on every installed Nano.

helpArticles.title: Weekly Test places all zones in test
helpArticles.summary: The start confirmation has a wider scope than testing just one selected zone.
helpArticles.body:
Use User → System → Weekly Test → Start/Stop, read the all-zones warning and confirm Yes. The panel identifies the next manual call point for the weekly test.

In this mode, a test fire sounds for five seconds before automatic silence, then resets five seconds later. The manual says plant equipment does not operate during Fire Test. The trainer makes the input activation and elapsed time visible, so the timing is learned rather than skipped.

Guided lessons pause the simulated clock, so reading the instructions cannot skip the five-second stages. Use the separately labelled FINDR time controls to advance them. Free practice runs the timers normally while visible.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Thinking Weekly Test affects only the next call point displayed on screen.

helpArticles.title: Leaving the screen is not the same as stopping Weekly Test
helpArticles.summary: Use the Start/Stop route again and confirm that all zones leave the test state.
helpArticles.body:
After testing, return to User → System → Weekly Test → Start/Stop. The stop confirmation explains that the zones will leave test. Confirm deliberately, then check the Test indication and active Test log.

Quit closes a displayed form or page; it does not by itself establish that every test condition has been removed. FINDR’s completion check requires the test state itself to be off.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Closing the weekly-test page and walking away while Test remains lit.

helpArticles.title: Use the separate Test field for one zone
helpArticles.summary: Zone Test and zone Disablement are distinct saved states.
helpArticles.body:
Open User → Zones, choose the intended zone and move to its Test field. Save Yes to place that zone in test; save No to remove it. The zone test behaviour follows the weekly-test description, but the scope is the selected zone.

Check Status separately. Setting Test to No does not mean the zone was re-enabled if its Status is Disabled. The tutorial leaves both settings in their intended final state.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Choosing Disabled when the intended exercise was a one-zone test.

helpArticles.title: DAY, NIGHT and NONE describe an override
helpArticles.summary: NONE hands control back to the commissioned settings.
helpArticles.body:
Use User → System → Day Night Mode. The form shows the control mode, current state and Level 2 Override. DAY requests day operation; NIGHT requests night operation; NONE removes the manual override and allows the commissioned schedule or settings to determine the state.

Night mode operates fire alarms without the day delay described in this manual. Day-mode delay durations and their period are site-specific. The practice fixture states its invented timing explicitly.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Reading NONE as an instruction to disable alarms or as a synonym for Night.

helpArticles.title: When does Next become Verify?
helpArticles.summary: Verify is available for a suitable fire-delay condition, with Delay active.
helpArticles.body:
The central button is normally Next for menus and form positions. In the relevant fire condition, the displayed Verify choice extends the alarm-delay sequence and lights the Verify indication.

Whether a delay applies to a particular input, how long it lasts and how escalation works depend on the commissioned cause and effect. FINDR labels its demonstration timings and does not claim that its illustrative settings belong to every Nano.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Pressing the centre button during a fire as though it were always a harmless next-menu action.

helpArticles.title: Zone and detector coincidence need their own interpretation
helpArticles.summary: The response to a first input differs between the two documented coincidence modes.
helpArticles.body:
The operator manual distinguishes zone coincidence from detector coincidence. For zone coincidence, a first detection can produce the indicated zone event and buzzer before a later detection produces the full fire response. Its detector-coincidence note describes a first-fire message without the same lamp and audible indications.

Exact group assignments and response rules are commissioned. This module keeps coincidence as reference material until a complete target-firmware configuration can be verified.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Applying the ordinary immediate-fire scenario to an unspecified coincidence configuration.

helpArticles.title: A channel is part of an interface device
helpArticles.summary: Use both the parent device and channel number to identify it.
helpArticles.body:
User → Loop → Channels displays channels of the four-channel interface devices. A channel label and current status are not the same thing as a detector’s zone assignment. The documented form also warns that Find can operate relay outputs.

The training fixture uses interface D4 with channels C1 to C4. Channel-status editing follows the same explicitly configured access assumption as device disablement. A real output action needs the site’s own cause-and-effect information; the trainer does not invent a live Find operation.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Treating D4 channel 2 as a separate device at address 2.

helpArticles.title: Loop status and Repair are separate
helpArticles.summary: Read the device count, wiring state and last found address before selecting an action.
helpArticles.body:
User → Loop → Status is an observation page. It reports the current loop status, number of devices, wiring status and the last device found. A displayed count is not an instruction to start allocation or change device addressing.

FINDR’s loop contains only its named training devices. The product’s larger allowed address range does not mean all addresses are populated.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Assuming a known device count alone proves there is no wiring fault.

helpArticles.title: Repair is for a wiring fault that has already been corrected
helpArticles.summary: The panel confirmation requires the physical fault to be cleared first.
helpArticles.body:
User → Loop → Repair displays a warning and Yes/No confirmation. The operator manual explicitly requires correction of the wiring fault before running Repair.

The lesson first retains a simulated loop fault, then lets you clear the invented fault cause using a labelled training control. Only then do you use the physical soft key to confirm Repair. This operation is separate from a fire Reset and does not alter the training device allocation.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Using Repair as though it can mend an open or shorted cable by itself.

helpArticles.title: Set the clock and check the event timestamps
helpArticles.summary: The clock form edits hours, minutes, date, month and year.
helpArticles.body:
Use Settings → System → Clock. Next advances to another time or date field; minus and plus adjust its value. Check the complete date and time before Save, because the historic record uses those values. Quit abandons the draft.

The demonstration date and allowed training calendar range are FINDR choices. Calendar validation prevents impossible dates; it is not a claim about the full firmware’s historical date range.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Changing the minute value while the hour field is still selected.

helpArticles.title: Read versions before comparing manuals
helpArticles.summary: Firmware and Site Data are separate read-only version pages.
helpArticles.body:
Customer Mode can view Engineering → System → Versions → Firmware and the neighbouring Site Data page. The Engineering branch name does not mean every item below it requires an engineering PIN.

Firmware identifies software components. Site Data identifies a configuration revision and update date. FINDR labels its software baseline and invented site-data values, so a trainee can tell source-backed behaviour from demonstration data.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Assuming the Site Data version is the main-controller firmware version.

helpArticles.title: What is simulated, and what needs a real-panel check?
helpArticles.summary: The controls operate a local fictional training state.
helpArticles.body:
The module teaches source-checked operator routes and makes configuration assumptions visible. It does not connect to a real fire panel. The practice building, event times, labels, PIN and timing fixture are invented.

V2.xx-only engineering procedures, printer operation, exact commissioning-tool behaviour and unresolved firmware differences stay labelled as reference material. Source links let you inspect the documents; a target-panel comparison is the next accuracy step.

Guided lessons pause simulated timers while you read; their labelled time controls advance the exercise. Free practice runs timers while the module is visible. The teaching pause is not presented as a Nano feature.
helpArticles.commonMistake: Treating a successful lesson as evidence that the same firmware and commissioning settings exist at an installation.

glossary.definition: A physical selection button whose current action is written above it on the LCD.
The authorised Access Level 2 operating mode reached using the site PIN.
The central navigation control; its verification-delay role applies only when that option is available.
Edited form values that need Save before the change is applied; Quit discards them.
An addressed loop point, identified by its address, label and type.
A detection grouping; the Nano zone form has separate Status and Test settings.
A configured grouping of alarm or plant outputs, with activation and enable states.
One input or output function within an interface device; identify both device and channel.
The addressing marker identified by a plus sign in the operator loop-map example.
A branch shown by indented devices in the illustrated loop map.
A currently present condition recorded in the relevant active log.
A retained record of a past operation or event; entry 1 is the newest.
A function deliberately or automatically out of service, requiring its own restoration action.
The additional amber indication for disabled alarm sectors, sounder devices or master alarms.
The documented test mode that places all zones in test after confirmation.
The single-zone Test setting, separate from that zone’s Enabled/Disabled status.
A manual DAY, NIGHT or NONE request controlling the panel’s commissioned day/night behaviour.
A further alarm delay selected in an applicable delayed-fire condition.
The panel’s configuration revision information, distinct from component firmware versions.
The confirmed panel operation performed after the underlying wiring fault has been corrected.

sourceGaps.title: Older detailed commissioning source
sourceGaps.detail: The detailed commissioning instructions are V2.xx issue 3 from May 2010; the selected operating and installation manuals are V3.xx. Engineering-only routes are not silently promoted to verified V3.xx firmware.
sourceGaps.impact: Operator routes are cross-checked against the V3.xx manual; unsupported engineering procedures remain reference-only.
sourceGaps.neededEvidence: A complete manufacturer V3.xx commissioning manual or a target-firmware menu recording.

sourceGaps.title: Device and channel status access
sourceGaps.detail: The V3.xx operator forms show read-only status, while older commissioning instructions document default Level 3 disablement with an optional Level 2 setting.
sourceGaps.impact: The training fixture explicitly selects the optional Customer Mode arrangement and labels these lessons configuration-dependent.
sourceGaps.neededEvidence: A V3.xx panel recording showing its access-control configuration and editable device/channel forms.

sourceGaps.title: Day-delay and coincidence settings
sourceGaps.detail: The selected operator manual describes day/night and verification roles but does not define a universal commissioned sequence for every input.
sourceGaps.impact: Demonstration settings are identified as FINDR choices; coincidence remains reference-only.
sourceGaps.neededEvidence: The intended real site cause-and-effect matrix, configured delays and a corresponding firmware capture.

sourceGaps.title: Physical Nano verification outstanding
sourceGaps.detail: The rendered face and procedures are based on manufacturer documents; no physical Nano has been compared button by button in this release.
sourceGaps.impact: The source baseline is visible and unresolved firmware behaviour is not represented as hardware-verified.
sourceGaps.neededEvidence: A complete recording of the selected Nano firmware, including navigation, prompts and outcomes.

sourceGaps.title: No printer attached in the practice fixture
sourceGaps.detail: Print is conditional on the printer arrangement and access level documented in the operator manual.
sourceGaps.impact: Printer routes are presented as conditional reference material rather than generating a real print job.
sourceGaps.neededEvidence: A compatible configured printer and a test of the target firmware’s print prompts.

sourceGaps.title: Practice calendar bounds
sourceGaps.detail: The manuals describe the clock form but do not supply a complete supported year-range and invalid-date behaviour contract.
sourceGaps.impact: The emulator validates dates within its declared training range and labels that bound as a FINDR choice.
sourceGaps.neededEvidence: Target-firmware validation of all calendar limits and field-boundary behaviour.

sourceGaps.title: Guided lessons pause the simulated clock
sourceGaps.detail: The manufacturer test durations describe real panel behaviour. FINDR pauses simulation time during guided lessons so the learner can read each instruction before explicitly advancing a timed stage.
sourceGaps.impact: Display and weekly-test lesson controls advance eight or five seconds deliberately. Free practice runs its timers while visible. No pause button is implied on real Nano hardware.
sourceGaps.neededEvidence: This is an explicit teaching policy, not an unresolved manufacturer claim.
